questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is defined as the amount of urine filtered by:
opts: All the nephrons in both kidneys in one minute
All nephrons of one kidney in one hour
The glomerular capillaries in one second
questions.exp: Definition: amount of urine filtered by all the nephrons in both kidneys in one minute. (Book p734)

questions.q: Fill up: GFR = net ultrafiltration pressure × the ultrafiltration (UF) ______.
questions.exp: GFR = net ultrafiltration pressure × ultrafiltration (UF) coefficient. (Book p734)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the GFR calculation is TRUE?
opts: Bowman's capsule pressure adds to filtration
Net ultrafiltration pressure = net hydrostatic pressure minus net oncotic pressure
Net ultrafiltration pressure = net oncotic pressure minus net hydrostatic pressure
The UF coefficient is subtracted from the net pressure
questions.exp: GFR = [net hydrostatic pressure (H.P) − net oncotic pressure (O.P)] × UF coefficient. (Book p734)

questions.q: In the expansion of the equation, the bracketed net hydrostatic pressure difference (glomerular capillary HP − Bowman's space HP) works out to:
questions.exp: (60 − 18) = 42 mmHg is the net hydrostatic term; the 10 mmHg net filtration pressure appears only after the 32 mmHg oncotic term is subtracted. (Book p734)

questions.q: Fill up: In the expansion of the oncotic term, the Bowman's space oncotic pressure is taken as ______.
questions.exp: (Glomerular capillary OP − Bowman's space OP) uses Bowman's space OP = 0. (Book p734)

questions.q: The ultrafiltration (UF) coefficient used in the book's worked GFR calculation is:
questions.exp: GFR = [(60 − 18) − (32 − 0)] × 12.5 ml/min/mmHg; the 10 mmHg net pressure is multiplied by this coefficient, not by 1.25 or 25. (Book p734)

questions.q: The net filtration pressure worked out on this page (the '= 10 × 12.5 ml/min' line, repeated in the boxes below the figure) is:
questions.exp: Net filtration pressure (10 mm Hg) = glomerular hydrostatic (60) − Bowman's capsule (18) − glomerular oncotic (32). (Book p734)

questions.q: Using [(60 − 18) − (32 − 0)] × 12.5 ml/min/mmHg, the book's calculated GFR is:
questions.exp: = 10 × 12.5 ml/min = 125 ml/min. (Book p734)

questions.q: Match each Starling pressure of the glomerulus with its book value — 1) Glomerular hydrostatic pressure 2) Bowman's capsule pressure 3) Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure … A) 32 mm Hg B) 60 mm Hg C) 18 mm Hg
questions.exp: Glomerular hydrostatic 60 mm Hg; Bowman's capsule 18 mm Hg; glomerular colloid osmotic 32 mm Hg. (Book p734)

questions.q: In the capillary–capsule diagram, the arrow drawn for Bowman's capsule pressure points back towards the glomerular capillary, i.e. it opposes filtration.
opts: True — it is subtracted in the calculation for exactly that reason
False — capsular pressure is shown favouring filtration
True — capsular pressure is one of the two forces that raise GFR
False — the diagram labels capsular pressure without any arrow
questions.exp: The 60 mmHg hydrostatic and 32 mmHg colloid osmotic arrows are drawn outwards from the capillary, while the 18 mmHg Bowman's capsule pressure arrow points back at it; hydrostatic favours and the other two oppose filtration. (Book p734)

questions.q: Fill up: In the glomerular figure, the vessel labelled on the left of the capillary tuft is the ______ arteriole and the one on the right is the efferent arteriole.
questions.exp: The figure labels 'Afferent arteriole' at the left and 'Efferent arteriole' at the right of the pink glomerular capillary, with the 60 mm Hg hydrostatic and 32 mm Hg colloid osmotic pressures inside it. (Book p734)

questions.q: All of these pressures appear in the boxed net filtration pressure equation on this page EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The box reads: net filtration pressure (10) = glomerular hydrostatic (60) − Bowman's capsule (18) − glomerular oncotic (32). The capsular oncotic pressure appears only in the written expansion above, where it is taken as zero. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: Normal GFR as written in the book is:
questions.exp: Normal GFR: 90–125 ml/min. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: The lower limit of the normal GFR range printed on this page is:
questions.exp: Normal GFR: 90–125 ml/min. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: The principal use of GFR listed is that:
opts: Chronic kidney disease is classified based on GFR
questions.exp: Use: chronic kidney disease (CKD) is classified based on GFR. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: As printed on this page, GFR is used both to stage acute kidney injury and to classify chronic kidney disease.
opts: False — the page says GFR has no staging role
False — only CKD classification is stated here
True — AKI stages are listed beside the G5 line
True — but only when the UF coefficient is normal
questions.exp: The 'Use' line states that chronic kidney disease (CKD) is classified based on GFR; no AKI staging appears on this page. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: Fill up: A GFR below 15 ml/min marks G5 / end-stage renal disease / the uremic phase, when ______ is required.
questions.exp: Eg: GFR <15 ml/min: G5/ESRD/uremic phase (dialysis required). (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: Which of the following statements about GFR staging is TRUE?
opts: GFR <15 ml/min corresponds to G2 CKD
GFR <15 ml/min needs no replacement therapy
GFR <15 ml/min corresponds to G5/ESRD, the uremic phase needing dialysis
questions.exp: GFR <15 ml/min = G5/ESRD/uremic phase, dialysis required. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: A 52-year-old with a GFR of 13 ml/min has nausea, pericardial rub and an uraemic rash. Applying this page's use of GFR, the patient is in:
opts: Not classifiable, since the page classifies only by creatinine
G5 / end-stage renal disease, the uremic phase — dialysis required
G4 CKD, where erythropoietin alone is the listed step
G3a CKD, where cystatin C must confirm before any decision
questions.exp: The page's single worked use of GFR is CKD classification: GFR <15 ml/min = G5/ESRD/uremic phase, dialysis required. (Book p734)

questions.sec: Normal GFR & its clinical use · p734
questions.q: Every one of these is a threshold or use stated on this page EXCEPT:
opts: CKD is classified on the basis of GFR
GFR <30 ml/min marks the uremic phase requiring dialysis
questions.exp: The dialysis-requiring uremic cut-off printed here is <15 ml/min; 30 ml/min is not the figure on this page. (Book p734)

questions.q: The best marker to estimate GFR is:
questions.exp: Creatinine: best marker to estimate GFR. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: Creatinine is produced in muscle from ______.
questions.exp: Produced in muscle from creatine; ↓ when muscle mass is reduced (eg: amputation). (Book p735)

questions.q: Serum creatinine falls when muscle mass is reduced; the book's example is:
questions.exp: ↓ sed when muscle mass reduced (eg: amputation). (Book p735)

questions.q: A bilateral above-knee amputee has a serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL although the true GFR is clearly reduced. Which property of creatinine printed here explains the normal value?
opts: Increased tubular secretion compensates for the loss
Dilution from post-operative fluids masks the rise
The assay under-reads in non-pregnant adults
Reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production
questions.exp: Creatinine is produced in muscle from creatine and is reduced when muscle mass is reduced — the book's own example is amputation, so a low production rate hides the fall in GFR. (Book p735)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about creatinine in pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Pregnancy raises the normal creatinine range to 1.5–2 mg/dL
Creatinine cannot be measured in pregnancy
Pregnancy is the only condition where high creatinine values are significant independently
Creatinine values lose all significance in pregnancy
questions.exp: Pregnancy: only condition where high creatinine values are significant independently (normal 0.3–0.6 mg/dL). (Book p735)

questions.q: The page marks pregnancy as the only condition in which high creatinine values are significant independently, with a normal range of 0.3–0.6 mg/dL.
opts: False — pregnancy never yields significant creatinine values
True — but the quoted range is 0.6–1.2 mg/dL
True — and the quoted pregnancy range is 0.3–0.6 mg/dL
False — the same independence is claimed for cirrhosis
questions.exp: Bullet: 'Pregnancy: Only condition where high creatinine values significant independently (Normal: 0.3–0.6 mg/dL)'. (Book p735)

questions.q: The normal creatinine range quoted for pregnancy is:
questions.exp: Normal in pregnancy: 0.3–0.6 mg/dL. (Book p735)

questions.q: Creatinine is described as a molecule of:
questions.exp: Bullet 4 prints '113 Kda molecule' — taught as printed (cystatin C on p737 is the 13 kDa protein). (Book p735)

questions.q: All of the following are stated about creatinine on this page EXCEPT:
opts: It is the best marker to estimate GFR
It is produced in muscle from creatine
Its value falls when muscle mass is reduced
questions.exp: Creatinine is printed as an 113 kDa molecule; 13 kDa is the cystatin C molecule described on p737. (Book p735)

questions.q: The Cockcroft & Gault equation is labelled in the book as:
opts: The only bedside formula still preferred
questions.exp: Cockcroft & Gault equation: obsolete; not preferred now due to disadvantages (though it is a bed-side formula). (Book p735)

questions.q: In the Cockcroft & Gault numerator, the patient's age is subtracted from:
questions.exp: Creatinine clearance = (140 − age) × body weight ÷ (72 × S.creatinine) in males. (Book p735)

questions.q: The denominator constant of the Cockcroft & Gault equation is:
questions.exp: Denominator: 72 × S.creatinine. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: In the Cockcroft & Gault creatinine clearance, the female result is the male formula multiplied by ______.
questions.exp: CrCl = (140−age) × BW / (72 × S.Cr) in males; × 0.8 in females. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: The book labels the Cockcroft & Gault equation as a ______ formula, which explains why it is still used despite being obsolete.
questions.exp: Two lines appear under the formula: 'Bed side formula' and 'Not preferred now d/t disadvantages'. (Book p735)

questions.q: The line printed directly under 'Bed side formula' says the Cockcroft & Gault equation is not preferred now because of its disadvantages.
opts: True — 'Not preferred now d/t disadvantages' is the next bullet
False — the next bullet says it is preferred in the ICU
True — but the stated reason is cost, not disadvantages
False — the page gives no reason for its obsolescence
questions.exp: Two bullets follow the formula: 'Bed side formula.' then 'Not preferred now d/t disadvantages.' — the disadvantages are then tabulated lower on the page. (Book p735)

questions.q: MDRD, as the page expands the abbreviation, is the society for:
opts: Measurement of drug dosing in renal disease
Mapping of dysfunction in renal dialysis
questions.exp: Entry 2 reads: MDRD equation — by society for modification of diet & renal diseases. (Book p735)

questions.q: Match each GFR equation with its origin — 1) MDRD equation 2) CKD-EPI equation 3) Schwartz equation … A) CKD-Epidemiology problem initiative group; best when GFR > 60 B) Society for modification of diet & renal diseases C) Estimates GFR in children
questions.exp: MDRD = society for modification of diet & renal diseases; CKD-EPI = CKD-Epidemiology problem initiative group (best when GFR > 60); Schwartz = children. (Book p735)

questions.q: The stated advantage of the CKD-EPI equation appears once the GFR is above:
questions.exp: CKD-EPI: Best (Advantage when GFR > 60). (Book p735)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about GFR equations is TRUE?
opts: MDRD and CKD-EPI are the preferred equations now
Cockcroft & Gault is the preferred equation now
Schwartz equation is used in adults only
questions.exp: MDRD and CKD-EPI are bracketed as 'preferred now'; CKD-EPI is best (advantage when GFR > 60). (Book p735)

questions.q: Match each equation with the label attached to it on this page — 1) Cockcroft & Gault 2) MDRD and CKD-EPI 3) CKD-EPI alone … A) Best when GFR is above 60 B) Obsolete, bed side formula C) Preferred now D) Used to estimate GFR in children
questions.exp: Cockcroft & Gault = obsolete bed side formula; MDRD and CKD-EPI are bracketed as 'Preferred now'; CKD-EPI alone carries 'Best (Advantage when GFR > 60)'. Schwartz is the children's equation. (Book p735)

questions.q: The table's first disadvantage says Cockcroft & Gault overestimates GFR because it assumes CrCl = GFR, which is only true for inert molecules such as:
questions.exp: Row 1, left column: 'Overestimate GFR: D/t assumption that CrCl = GFR (Only true for inert molecules like inulin).' (Book p735)

questions.q: Because creatinine is secreted, the book writes creatinine clearance as:
opts: GFR + tubular secretion (or GFR − tubular absorption)
questions.exp: Cr is secreted → CrCl = GFR + tubular secretion (clearance = GFR + tubular secretion or GFR − tubular absorption). (Book p735)

questions.q: According to the table, the Cockcroft & Gault equation overestimates GFR because creatinine is filtered and also secreted.
opts: False — the page says it underestimates GFR for the same reason
True — because alkaline picrate assays under-read creatinine
False — tubular secretion only affects IDMs-based assays
True — clearance equals GFR plus tubular secretion
questions.exp: The disadvantage column lists 'Cr is secreted → CrCl = GFR + Tubular secretion', alongside clearance = GFR + secretion or GFR − absorption, which is why the estimate over-reads true GFR. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: Opposite the 'Overestimate GFR' row, the advantage of the MDRD & CKD-EPI equations is that they ______ GFR.
questions.exp: Row 1, right column of the table reads simply 'Directly measures GFR.' (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: The Cockcroft & Gault equation was developed when creatinine was estimated by the ______ method, a colorimetric assay using alkaline picrate.
questions.exp: The disadvantage table states the equation was developed when Cr was estimated by Jaffe's method: colorimetric assay using alkaline picrate, flagged as not a standard method. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: The MDRD/CKD-EPI equations estimate creatinine with standard assays, namely ______ (isotope dilution mass spectroscopy).
questions.exp: Advantage row 2: 'Equation uses estimation of Cr using standard assays: IDM. (Isotope dilution mass spectrosopy)' — the scan misspells spectroscopy; taught as printed. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: The last disadvantage listed for the Cockcroft & Gault equation is over emphasis on ______.
questions.exp: Row 3, left column: 'Over emphasis on BW.' — the matching advantage cell says race is used instead of weight. (Book p735)

questions.q: All of the following are disadvantages of the Cockcroft & Gault equation EXCEPT:
opts: It was developed when Cr was estimated by Jaffe's alkaline-picrate method
It uses race instead of weight
It overestimates GFR by assuming CrCl = GFR
Creatinine secretion makes CrCl = GFR + tubular secretion
questions.exp: Using race instead of weight is an advantage of MDRD/CKD-EPI; C&G over-emphasises BW, overestimates GFR and rests on Jaffe's method. (Book p735)

questions.q: Equation 4 on this page, the Schwartz equation, is used to estimate GFR in:
questions.exp: 4. Schwartz equation: Estimate GFR in children — its formula and constants continue on the next page. (Book p735)

questions.q: Fill up: The Schwartz equation computes eGFR as K × the child's ______ divided by S.Cr.
questions.exp: eGFR = K × length of child / S.Cr. (Book p736)

questions.q: The Schwartz equation printed here estimates a child's GFR from body surface area divided by serum creatinine.
opts: False — it uses weight rather than length
False — it is K × length of the child ÷ S.Cr
True — BSA is the numerator of the printed formula
questions.exp: The line reads: eGFR = K × length of child ÷ S.Cr, with K described as a constant. (Book p736)

questions.q: In the Schwartz equation, the constant K for a term infant under 1 year (age not mentioned) is:
questions.exp: <1 yr: pre-term 0.33, term 0.45 (if age not mentioned). (Book p736)

questions.q: Match each child group with its Schwartz constant K — 1) Pre-term <1 yr 2) Term <1 yr 3) 1–2 yr and adolescent girls 4) Adolescent boys … A) 0.45 B) 0.33 C) 0.7 D) 0.55
questions.exp: K: pre-term 0.33; term 0.45; 1–2 yr & adolescent girls 0.55; adolescent boys 0.7. (Book p736)

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy and a 14-year-old girl of identical height and identical serum creatinine are assessed with the Schwartz equation. Per the printed K values, the boy's eGFR will be:
opts: Higher, because K is 0.7 in adolescent boys versus 0.55 in adolescent girls
Lower, because K is 0.55 in adolescent boys
The same, since K varies with height and not with sex
Undefined, because K is printed only below 2 years of age
questions.exp: The K constants are listed as: <1 yr pre-term 0.33, term 0.45; 1–2 yr & adolescent girls 0.55; adolescent boys 0.7. (Book p736)

questions.q: Each Schwartz constant is paired with the correct group EXCEPT:
opts: Term infant <1 yr, age not mentioned — 0.45
questions.exp: The 1–2 yr and adolescent girls line carries K = 0.55; 0.45 is the term infant value used when the age is not mentioned. (Book p736)

questions.q: The constant K in this equation is changed according to:
questions.exp: K is tabulated by developmental group: pre-term, term, 1–2 yr and adolescent girls, adolescent boys — i.e. age plus sex, not any measured variable. (Book p736)

questions.q: In acute kidney injury, creatinine takes how long to start rising?
questions.exp: Disadvantage 1: 24–48 hrs to start rising in AKI. (Book p736)

questions.q: Six hours after a crush injury the serum creatinine is still 0.9 mg/dL although urine output has fallen. Which line on this page accounts for that?
opts: Creatinine is reabsorbed by the tubule in injury
Muscle mass drops instantly, normalising the value
Trauma increases tubular secretion of creatinine
Creatinine takes 24–48 hrs to start rising in AKI
questions.exp: Disadvantage 1 reads: 24–48 hrs to start rising in Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) — an early normal creatinine does not exclude AKI. (Book p736)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about creatinine determinants is TRUE as written in the book?
opts: Creatinine is lower in African Americans
Creatinine is higher in African Americans
Creatinine rises after 40 years of age
Creatinine is independent of muscle mass
questions.exp: Determinants as written: muscle mass (↓ muscle mass → ↓ Cr), race (↓ in African Americans), age (↓ after 40 years d/t ↓ muscle mass) and sex (↓ in males). (Book p736)

questions.q: Fill up: Creatinine falls after 40 years of age because of the decline in ______.
questions.exp: Age (↓ after 40 years d/t ↓ in muscle mass). (Book p736)

questions.q: Serum creatinine declines with age after which point, because muscle mass falls?
questions.exp: Dependent on: Age (↓ after 40 years d/t ↓ in muscle mass). (Book p736)

questions.q: In the 'Dependent on' list, the page prints the sex line as 'Sex (↓ in males)'.
opts: True — the printed wording is ↓ in males
False — the page reads ↓ in females
True — and race carries the identical downward arrow for males
False — sex is not one of the listed determinants
questions.exp: The four bullets are muscle mass (↓ muscle mass → ↓ Cr), race (↓ in African Americans), age (↓ after 40 years d/t ↓ in muscle mass) and sex (↓ in males). The print is quoted verbatim; physiologically greater male muscle mass gives HIGHER creatinine, so this line is a flagged source caveat. (Book p736)

questions.q: Fill up: Reduced protein supplementation and malnutrition both lower serum creatinine by decreasing ______.
questions.exp: Diet alters S.Cr: ↓ protein supplementation → ↓ muscle mass → ↓ S.Cr, and malnutrition → ↓ muscle mass → ↓ S.Cr. (Book p736)

questions.q: Fill up: In obesity there is no change in S.Cr because ______ does not affect S.Cr.
questions.exp: Obesity: no change in S.Cr as fat doesn't affect S.Cr. (Book p736)

questions.q: Creatinine is dependent on all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Dependent on muscle mass, race, age and sex; obesity causes no change in S.Cr as fat doesn't affect S.Cr. (Book p736)

questions.q: Fill up: Cimetidine and trimethoprim raise serum creatinine by competing with Cr for tubular ______.
questions.exp: They compete with Cr for tubular secretion → ↓ tubular secretion of Cr → ↑ serum Cr. (Book p736)

questions.q: Cimetidine and trimethoprim raise the serum creatinine through every step of the printed flowchart EXCEPT:
opts: Competition with creatinine for tubular secretion
questions.exp: The flow reads: compete with Cr for tubular secretion → ↓ tubular secretion of Cr → ↑ serum Cr; secretion falls rather than rises. (Book p736)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the GFR–creatinine relationship is TRUE?
opts: An initial creatinine rise corresponds to a trivial GFR fall
By the time creatinine rises, GFR has already fallen significantly
Creatinine rises before any fall in GFR
questions.exp: Inverse relationship: by the time Cr rises GFR falls significantly; the initial rise in Cr corresponds to a significant fall in GFR. (Book p736)

questions.q: On the inverse-relationship graph, by the time S.Cr reaches 2 mg/dL the GFR has fallen to about:
questions.exp: By the time S.Cr = 2, GFR falls to ~60 ml/min. (Book p736)

questions.q: A dialysis-dependent patient's creatinine rises from 5 to 20 mg/dL over a month. Per the page's reading of the inverse curve:
opts: GFR is unchanged, because the curve is linear in this range
The fall in GFR is insignificant — the patient was already in ESRD
GFR has fallen from 50 to 30 ml/min
GFR has halved from 60 to 30 ml/min
questions.exp: Worked example: ↑ S.Cr from 5 to 20 → fall in GFR is insignificant (patient was already in ESRD), whereas 1.7 → 2.8 marks 50 → 30 ml/min. (Book p736)

questions.q: A patient's serum creatinine rises from 1.7 to 2.8 mg/dL. Per the book's inverse-relationship examples, this rise means the GFR has:
opts: Fallen insignificantly because the patient was already in ESRD
questions.exp: ↑ in S.Cr from 1.7 to 2.8: GFR falls significantly (50 ml/min → 30 ml/min); the 5→20 example is the insignificant one (already ESRD). (Book p736)

questions.q: The page states that a rise in serum creatinine from 1.7 to 2.8 mg/dL corresponds to a fall in GFR from about 50 to about 30 ml/min.
opts: True — this is the second worked example under the curve
False — this rise is described as insignificant
True — and the same is said for a rise from 5 to 20 mg/dL
False — the pair quoted for this range is 125 to 100 ml/min
questions.exp: Both examples sit under the graph: S.Cr 1.7 → 2.8 gives GFR 50 → 30 ml/min (significant fall), while 5 → 20 is insignificant in established ESRD. (Book p736)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Fill up: Whole-kidney GFR equals single nephron GFR multiplied by the ______ of nephrons.
questions.exp: GFR = single nephron GFR × number of nephrons. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Fill up: The label written on the arrow between the compensatory rise in snGFR and intraglomerular hypertension is 'Beyond point of ______'.
questions.exp: The vertical arrow in the note is captioned 'Beyond point of compensation', after which intraglomerular HTN follows. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Which sequence matches the book's hyperfiltration-injury note?
opts: ↓ nephron number → ↑ snGFR to maintain GFR → beyond compensation intraglomerular HTN → proteinuria → interstitial fibrosis → ↓ GFR
questions.exp: Even if number ↓, snGFR ↑ to maintain GFR (hyperfiltration injury); beyond the point of compensation: intraglomerular HTN → proteinuria → interstitial fibrosis → ↓ GFR. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: The order of arrows in the hyperfiltration note on this page is:
opts: ↑ snGFR → intraglomerular HTN → proteinuria → interstitial fibrosis → ↓ GFR
↑ snGFR → proteinuria → intraglomerular HTN → ↓ GFR → fibrosis
questions.exp: GFR = snGFR × number of nephrons; when nephron number falls, snGFR rises to maintain GFR (hyperfiltration injury) → beyond point of compensation → intraglomerular HTN → proteinuria → interstitial fibrosis → ↓ GFR. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Fill up: Clearance equals urine concentration × urine volume (V) divided by the ______ concentration.
questions.exp: Clearance = (urine concentration × volume of urine in ml/min (V)) / plasma concentration. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: In the clearance formula printed here, V stands for:
opts: Volume of urine in ml/24 h
questions.exp: Clearance = urine concentration × volume of urine in ml/min (V) ÷ plasma concentration. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Endogenous creatinine clearance is written as:
questions.exp: Endogenous Cr clearance = U_cr × V / P_cr. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Fill up: Endogenous creatinine clearance is written on this page as U_cr × V divided by ______.
questions.exp: Endogenous Cr clearance = (U_cr × V) / P_cr, the generic clearance formula applied to creatinine. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Match each cystatin C fact with its descriptor — 1) Size 2) Biochemical class 3) Production … A) Constant rate by all nucleated cells B) 13 kDa molecule protein C) Cysteine protease inhibitor
questions.exp: Cystatin C: 13 kDa molecule protein; cysteine protease inhibitor; produced at constant rate by all nucleated cells. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: All of the following describe cystatin C handling EXCEPT:
opts: It is reabsorbed by the PCT
It is produced at a constant rate
It is secreted by the PCT
It is filtered but not secreted
questions.exp: Cystatin C: filtered but not secreted; reabsorbed by PCT; constant production — it is never secreted. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Every statement about cystatin C matches the page EXCEPT:
opts: It is a cysteine protease inhibitor
It is produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells
It is filtered and then secreted by the tubule
It is a 13 kDa molecule protein
questions.exp: The bullets read: filtered but not secreted, reabsorbed by PCT; the other three lines are printed as such. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Cystatin C is reabsorbed by the proximal convoluted tubule but is not secreted by it.
opts: True — and for that reason it replaces creatinine as the marker
True — both handling lines appear under the cystatin C heading
False — it is secreted by the PCT and not reabsorbed
False — it is neither filtered nor reabsorbed
questions.exp: The two right-hand bullets state 'Filtered but not secreted' and 'Reabsorbed by PCT'; the page nevertheless ends with 'cannot replace Cr'. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Cystatin C is not affected by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Advantages: not affected by race, diet, muscle mass or drugs; inflammation (with steroids and smoking) elevates it non-specifically. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Cystatin C is explicitly listed as NOT affected by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The 'Not affected by' block lists race, diet, muscle mass and drugs; inflammation is in the 'Non specifically elevated in' block instead, along with taking steroids and smoking. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Cystatin C is non-specifically elevated in inflammation, smokers and patients:
questions.exp: Non specifically elevated in: inflammation, taking steroids, smokers. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Fill up: Because of its non-specific elevations, cystatin C cannot replace ______.
questions.exp: Therefore, cannot replace Cr. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: A 70-year-old amputee on long-term steroids for asthma needs a GFR estimate. Applying this page, ordering cystatin C is best described as:
opts: Equivalent to creatinine, which is unaffected by amputation
Useful for the muscle-mass problem, but steroids raise it non-specifically
Ideal, since cystatin C is unaffected by drug therapy
Pointless, since cystatin C also depends on muscle mass
questions.exp: Advantages: not affected by race, diet, muscle mass or drugs; disadvantages: non-specifically elevated in inflammation, taking steroids and smokers — hence it cannot replace creatinine. (Book p737)

questions.sec: Note, endogenous clearance & Cystatin C · p737
questions.q: Match each cystatin C property with the consequence the page draws from it — 1) Constant production by all nucleated cells 2) Filtered, not secreted, reabsorbed by PCT 3) Raised in inflammation, steroids and smokers … A) Non-specific elevation, so it cannot replace creatinine B) Independent of muscle mass and diet C) Its clearance reflects GFR rather than tubular handling
questions.exp: Constant nucleated-cell production is what frees it from the muscle-mass and diet dependence of creatinine; being filtered without secretion makes it a GFR marker; the non-specific elevations are why the page says it cannot replace Cr. (Book p737)

questions.q: The renal autoregulation range of mean arterial pressure is:
questions.exp: Within auto regulation range (MAP: 80–180 mmHg); 40–240 is only the graph axis. (Book p738)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about renal autoregulation is TRUE?
opts: Within the autoregulation range RBF and GFR are constant
Within the range RBF rises linearly with pressure
GFR falls to zero within the range
questions.exp: Renal blood flow (RBF) and GFR are constant within the autoregulation range. (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: The first mechanism of renal autoregulation, put in brackets as the stretch reflex, is the ______ reflex.
questions.exp: Mechanism: 1. myogenic reflex (stretch reflex); 2. tubulo-glomerular feedback (adenosine mediated). (Book p738)

questions.q: Match each autoregulation mechanism with its descriptor — 1) Myogenic reflex 2) Tubulo glomerular feedback … A) Adenosine mediated B) Stretch reflex
questions.exp: Mechanisms: myogenic reflex (stretch reflex) and tubulo glomerular feedback (adenosine mediated). (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: In response to a falling GFR (eg: pre-renal failure), the afferent arteriole undergoes ______, raising filtration.
questions.exp: In response to ↓ GFR → afferent arteriolar vasodilatation → ↑ filtration. (Book p738)

questions.q: A patient in pre-renal failure has a falling GFR. Per the left branch of this page's flowchart, the afferent arteriolar response and its effect are:
opts: No response, since autoregulation only answers a raised MAP
questions.exp: In response to ↓ GFR the flowchart shows afferent arteriolar vasodilatation (eg: pre-renal failure) → ↑ filtration; the adenosine branch belongs to ↑ GFR/tubular injury. (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: With ↑ GFR/tubular injury, more NaCl/KCl reaches the macula densa and releases ______, causing afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.
questions.exp: ↑ NaCl/KCl reach macula densa → adenosine → afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction → ↓ filtration. (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: In the macula densa arm of the flowchart, the rising luminal solute is written as increased NaCl/______ reaching the macula densa.
questions.exp: The printed line is '↑ GFR/tubular injury → ↑ NaCl/KCl reach macula densa', followed by adenosine and afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. (Book p738)

questions.q: Match each branch of the autoregulation flowchart with its printed example or mediator — 1) Response to ↓ GFR 2) ↑ GFR/tubular injury 3) Mediator of tubulo-glomerular feedback … A) Adenosine B) Pre-renal failure C) Acute tubular injury D) Stretch reflex
questions.exp: The ↓ GFR branch is illustrated by pre-renal failure; the ↑ GFR/tubular injury branch is illustrated by acute tubular injury and runs through adenosine; the stretch reflex is the myogenic mechanism, a different item. (Book p738)

questions.q: On the autoregulation graph, the vertical dashed lines that bracket the plateau are drawn on which axis, and between which values?
opts: Renal plasma flow, between 125 and 700 ml/min
Mean arterial blood pressure, between about 80 and 180 mm Hg
Mean arterial blood pressure, between 0 and 40 mm Hg
questions.exp: The plot's x-axis is mean arterial blood pressure (0–240 mm Hg) with the 'autoregulatory range' double arrow spanning roughly 80–180, over the flat portion of the renal blood flow curve. (Book p738)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about glomerulo-tubular balance is TRUE?
opts: Reabsorption stays fixed while excretion rises
The percentage of Na+ excreted remains constant as reabsorption compensates
The percentage of Na+ excreted doubles when GFR doubles
questions.exp: ↑ GFR → ↑ reabsorption by tubule (compensation) → % of Na+ excreted remains constant (1% in both examples). (Book p738)

questions.q: In the glomerulo-tubular balance example with GFR = 100 ml/min, the filtered Na+ load and the excreted amount are:
questions.exp: GFR = 100 ml/min → Na+ filtered = 100 meq → 99 meq reabsorbed, 1 meq excreted (1%). (Book p738)

questions.q: In the glomerulo-tubular balance example at GFR = 200 ml/min, the amounts reabsorbed and excreted are:
questions.exp: GFR 200: Na+ filtered 200 meq → 198 meq reabsorbed, 2 meq excreted (1%). (Book p738)

questions.q: Each of the following is part of the page's glomerulo-tubular balance account EXCEPT:
opts: In the second example 198 meq are reabsorbed and 2 meq excreted, still labelled 1%
The percentage of filtered sodium excreted rises as GFR rises
An increase in GFR is followed by increased tubular reabsorption
questions.exp: The whole point of the balance is that the percentage of Na+ excreted remains constant at 1%; the doubling example on the page is GFR 200 ml/min with 200 meq filtered, 198 reabsorbed and 2 meq excreted. (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: The numerator of the printed fraction 125/700 is the ______.
questions.exp: The worked line is = 125 / 700 = 0.1 to 0.2, i.e. GFR over renal plasma flow. (Book p738)

questions.q: The renal plasma flow used as the denominator of the filtration fraction on this page is given as:
questions.exp: FF = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow, with the note RPF = 700 ml, estimated using para amino hippuric acid (PAH). (Book p738)

questions.q: Fill up: Renal plasma flow (700 ml) is estimated using para amino hippuric acid, abbreviated ______.
questions.exp: RPF = 700 ml: estimated using para amino hippuric acid (PAH). (Book p738)

questions.q: The filtration fraction computed as 125/700 equals:
Filtration fraction computed as 125/700 is stated on the page as:
Fill up: A raised filtration fraction increases peritubular capillary oncotic pressure, taking fluid from the interstitial space and lowering renal interstitial ______, which boosts PCT reabsorption.
questions.exp: ↑ FF → ↑ peritubular capillary OP → taken-in fluid from interstitial space → ↓ renal interstitial HP (RIHP) → ↑ reabsorption from PCT. (Book p738)

questions.q: Following the arrows for a raised filtration fraction, the correct sequence on this page is:
opts: ↑ reabsorption from PCT → ↓ filtration fraction → ↑ renal interstitial HP
↑ peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → fluid taken from the interstitial space → ↓ renal interstitial HP → ↑ reabsorption from PCT
↑ renal interstitial HP → ↑ peritubular oncotic pressure → ↓ reabsorption from PCT
↓ peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → ↑ renal interstitial HP → ↓ reabsorption
questions.exp: ↑ FF → ↑ peritubular capillary OP (d/t more filtration) → taken in fluid from interstitial space → ↓ RIHP → ↑ reabsorption from PCT. (Book p738)

questions.q: A cirrhotic patient with low effective arterial volume has a raised filtration fraction. Applying this page's chain, proximal tubular reabsorption is expected to:
opts: Increase, because peritubular capillary oncotic pressure is high while interstitial pressure is low
Decrease, because interstitial hydrostatic pressure is low
Increase, because the PCT oncotic pressure falls
Remain unchanged, as filtration fraction does not touch reabsorption
questions.exp: The chain drawn under filtration fraction links a raised FF to higher peritubular capillary oncotic pressure, removal of fluid from the interstitium, a fall in RIHP and therefore increased PCT reabsorption. (Book p738)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about pressure natriuresis is TRUE?
opts: A raised cardiac output increases excretion of Na+ and H2O
A raised cardiac output decreases sodium excretion
questions.exp: ↑ CO leads to ↑ excretion of Na+ & H2O; therefore ↑ CO cannot produce sustained ↑ BP unless there is renal impairment. (Book p738)

questions.q: The book's pressure-natriuresis caveat uses which blood-pressure identity?
questions.exp: Therefore, ↑ CO cannot produce sustained ↑ in BP unless there is renal impairment (BP = CO × PVR). (Book p738)

questions.q: The printed theory of pressure natriuresis concludes that a raised cardiac output cannot produce a sustained rise in blood pressure unless there is renal impairment.
opts: False — a raised cardiac output sustains pressure whatever the kidney does
True — and the page writes the identity as BP = CO ÷ PVR
False — the theory concerns water diuresis only, not sodium
True — the sentence is written immediately after the ↑CO line
questions.exp: As printed: ↑ CO leads to ↑ excretion of Na+ & H2O; therefore ↑ CO cannot produce sustained ↑ in BP unless there is renal impairment (BP = CO × PVR). (Book p738)

questions.q: Match each step of the pressure-natriuresis mechanism with what follows — 1) ↑ CO 2) ↓ Reabsorption from PCT 3) ↑ Medullary blood flow … A) ↑ Na+ & H2O excretion B) ↑ RBF C) ↑ RIHP
questions.exp: ↑ CO → ↑ RBF → ↓ reabsorption from PCT → ↑ RIHP → ↑ medullary blood flow → ↑ Na+ & H2O excretion. (Book p739)

questions.q: The mechanism chain for pressure natriuresis continued on this page runs in which order?
opts: ↑ CO → ↓ RBF → ↑ reabsorption from PCT → ↓ medullary blood flow
↑ CO → ↑ reabsorption from PCT → ↓ RIHP → ↑ Na+ excretion
↑ CO → ↑ RBF → ↓ reabsorption from PCT → ↑ RIHP → ↑ medullary blood flow → ↑ Na+ & H2O excretion
questions.exp: The printed arrows are: ↑ CO → ↑ RBF → ↓ reabsorption from PCT → ↑ RIHP → ↑ medullary blood flow, which then feeds down to ↑ Na+ & H2O excretion. (Book p739)

questions.q: Every step below appears in this page's pressure-natriuresis chain EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The chain lists only cardiac output, RBF, PCT reabsorption, RIHP, medullary blood flow and the resulting Na+ and water excretion; aldosterone is not part of it. (Book p739)

questions.q: Fill up: In the chain, the rise in medullary blood flow is immediately followed by increased excretion of ______.
questions.exp: The terminal arrow of the flowchart points to ↑ Na+ & H2O excretion. (Book p739)

questions.q: Compared with the filtration-fraction chain on p738, the pressure-natriuresis chain on this page moves renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure in the opposite direction.
opts: True — and in both chains the final effect is increased PCT reabsorption
True — a raised filtration fraction lowers RIHP here while pressure natriuresis raises it
False — both chains show RIHP rising
False — both chains show RIHP falling
questions.exp: p738: ↑FF → ↑peritubular capillary OP → fluid taken from the interstitium → ↓RIHP → ↑PCT reabsorption. p739: ↑CO → ↑RBF → ↓PCT reabsorption → ↑RIHP → ↑medullary blood flow. The RIHP arrows point opposite ways, and the reabsorption arrows also oppose. (Book p739)

questions.q: Fill up: Afferent arteriolar dilatation in the hemodynamics list is mediated by ______.
questions.exp: Afferent arteriolar dilatation (mediated by prostaglandins). (Book p739)

questions.q: Fill up: Efferent arteriolar constriction in the hemodynamics list is mediated by ______.
questions.exp: Efferent arteriolar constriction (mediated by angiotensin II). (Book p739)

questions.q: All of the following are listed arteriolar events in the glomerular-hemodynamics section EXCEPT:
opts: Afferent arteriolar dilatation mediated by prostaglandins
Efferent arteriolar constriction mediated by angiotensin II
Afferent arteriolar constriction mediated by angiotensin II
questions.exp: The book pairs afferent dilatation with prostaglandins and efferent constriction with angiotensin II; afferent constriction carries no angiotensin-II label. (Book p739)

questions.q: Each statement about the mediators listed under glomerular hemodynamics is correct EXCEPT:
opts: Afferent arteriolar constriction is listed without any mediator
Efferent arteriolar dilatation is mediated by prostaglandins
Afferent arteriolar dilatation is mediated by prostaglandins
Efferent arteriolar constriction is mediated by angiotensin II
questions.exp: Only two of the four arteriolar events carry a mediator: afferent dilatation (prostaglandins) and efferent constriction (angiotensin II); the two constriction/dilatation counterparts are printed unqualified. (Book p739)

questions.q: Fill up: In the 'Control' diagram of the table, the vessel entering the glomerulus on the left is labelled ______.
questions.exp: The control drawing is captioned Glomerulus with Afferent written at the left limb and Efferent at the right limb. (Book p739)

questions.q: Match each arteriolar resistance change with its renal-blood-flow and net-ultrafiltration-pressure pair — 1) Increased afferent 2) Decreased afferent 3) Increased efferent 4) Decreased efferent … A) RBF ↑, NUP ↑ (favourable for kidney) B) RBF ↓, NUP ↓ (unfavourable) C) RBF ↓, NUP ↑ (unfavourable) D) RBF ↑, NUP ↓ (unfavourable)
questions.exp: Table: increased afferent ↓↓; decreased afferent ↑↑ (favourable); increased efferent ↓↑; decreased efferent ↑↓ — all but decreased afferent are unfavourable. (Book p739)

questions.q: Which row of the arteriolar-resistance table is annotated 'Favourable for kidney'?
questions.exp: The word 'Favourable for kidney' is written level with the decreased-afferent row, whose arrows show renal blood flow and net ultrafiltration pressure both rising. (Book p739)

questions.q: The annotation 'unfavourable' appears twice in the table: beside increased afferent resistance and beside decreased efferent resistance.
opts: True — and both rows raise net ultrafiltration pressure
True — both of those rows drive net ultrafiltration pressure down
False — only the increased afferent row carries that word
False — increased efferent resistance is also marked unfavourable
questions.exp: 'unfavourable' is printed against increased afferent (↓ flow, ↓ ultrafiltration pressure) and against decreased efferent (↑ flow, ↓ ultrafiltration pressure); increased efferent is left unlabelled and decreased afferent is the favourable row. (Book p739)

questions.q: Match each row of the table with the pair of arrows printed for it — 1) Increased efferent 2) Decreased efferent 3) Increased afferent … A) Renal blood flow ↓, net ultrafiltration pressure ↑ B) Renal blood flow ↑, net ultrafiltration pressure ↓ C) Renal blood flow ↓, net ultrafiltration pressure ↓
questions.exp: Increased efferent resistance is the only row where flow falls while net ultrafiltration pressure rises; decreasing it does the reverse; increasing afferent resistance lowers both. (Book p739)

questions.q: Efferent arteriolar constriction reduces blood flow to the medulla and causes:
questions.exp: Efferent arteriolar constriction → ↓ blood flow to medulla → medullary hypoxia. (Book p739)

questions.q: In the normal-blood-flow note, the sequence after the efferent arteriole is:
opts: Glomerular capillary → vasa recta → peritubular capillary
Peritubular capillary → vasa recta → renal medulla
Vasa recta → peritubular capillary → renal cortex
Peritubular capillary → renal pelvis → vasa recta
questions.exp: Efferent arteriole → peritubular capillary → vasa recta → renal medulla. (Book p739)

questions.q: The line 'Efferent arteriole → peritubular capillary → vasa recta → renal medulla' appears under which heading?
questions.exp: It is written as 'Note: Normal blood flow', immediately after the efferent-constriction → medullary hypoxia line. (Book p739)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about ACE inhibitors is TRUE per the book?
opts: ACE inhibitors are harmful in all nephrology patients
Blocking angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering GFR (↑S.Cr) but raising blood flow
ACE inhibitors constrict the efferent arteriole
ACE inhibitors raise GFR by dilating the afferent arteriole
questions.exp: ACE inhibitor: block angiotensin II → efferent arteriolar dilatation → ↓ GFR (↑S.Cr) but ↑ blood flow; beneficial for nephrology patients. (Book p739)

questions.q: An ACE inhibitor is called 'beneficial for nephrology patients' on this page despite lowering GFR. The stated reason to continue is that efferent arteriolar dilatation:
opts: Reverses medullary hypoxia by constricting the efferent arteriole
Increases blood flow while creatinine rises with the fall in GFR
Raises net ultrafiltration pressure and so improves filtration
questions.exp: The ACE-inhibitor block reads: block angiotensin II → efferent arteriolar dilatation → ↓ GFR (↑S.Cr) but ↑ blood flow. (Book p739)

questions.q: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on an ACE inhibitor and deteriorates. The book's explanation is that:
opts: The afferent arteriole is not working and the efferent arteriole was maintaining GFR
The efferent arteriole was already fully dilated
Prostaglandins were blocking the afferent arteriole
questions.exp: C/I in patients with b/l renal artery stenosis: afferent arteriole not working, efferent arteriole maintains GFR — removing angiotensin II collapses that support. (Book p739)

questions.q: Fill up: NSAIDs block prostaglandins and thereby block ______ arteriolar dilatation, leaving efferent constriction to lower GFR and RBF.
questions.exp: NSAID: block prostaglandins → block afferent arteriolar dilatation → efferent arteriolar constriction → ↓ GFR & ↓ RBF. (Book p739)

questions.q: A cirrhotic patient with ascites is given indomethacin and urine output falls. The NSAID block on this page explains this as:
opts: Medullary blood flow rises, washing out the gradient
Renal interstitial pressure falls, increasing reabsorption
Prostaglandins blocked → afferent dilatation blocked, leaving efferent constriction, so GFR and RBF fall
Angiotensin II blocked → efferent dilatation, so filtration falls
questions.exp: Printed chain: Block prostaglandins → block afferent arteriolar dilatation → efferent arteriolar constriction → ↓ GFR & ↓ RBF. A back-arrow from '↓ GFR & ↓ RBF' to 'maintain GFR' is also drawn on the page; its intent is not explained and is flagged as a source caveat. (Book p739)

questions.q: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients already on ACE inhibitors because blocking angiotensin II removes efferent constriction and precipitates:
questions.exp: C/I in patients on ACE(−): ACEI → efferent arteriolar constriction blocked → frank renal failure. (Book p739)
